scenarios.title: New platform lead inherits a fragile cloud
scenarios.prompt: I just became platform lead for a ~600-compute OpenStack cloud. The previous team mostly left. There are frequent incidents, people restart things when in doubt, upgrades have been postponed for years, and engineers who joined with me already want to migrate to a new deployment tool and redesign networking. Where do I start?
missing_information: maintenance status of the running series
what documentation, recovery procedures and vendors exist
expected_reasoning: advises restraint: do not start by transforming the platform
follows Discover, Protect, Assess, Stabilize, Recover knowledge, Simplify, Establish control, Evolve
lists first-30-day outputs: current-state map, critical risks, guardrails, ownership gaps, recovery gaps, control roadmap
guardrails each with owner and removal condition
notes the exception: if the series is so far behind that it is unpatched, transformation of the release may be the stabilization
starts from business capabilities rather than components
expected_output: phased plan with first-30-day deliverables, guardrails table, exit criteria
critical_errors: endorses starting with the deployment tool migration and network redesign
proposes a single maturity score as the outcome
criteria: Advises against immediate transformation and explains why
Uses the restoration sequence or an equivalent staged approach
Requires owners and removal conditions for guardrails
Mentions the exception for unmaintained, vulnerable releases

scenarios.title: Senior engineer leaves in four weeks
scenarios.prompt: Our most senior OpenStack engineer leaves in 4 weeks. He did every upgrade and knows why half our customizations exist. Management asked him to write documentation and do two knowledge-transfer presentations. Is that enough?
available_evidence: he knows reasons for many customizations (reported)
missing_information: test environment availability for upgrade rehearsal
expected_reasoning: states that presentations prove a session took place, not transfer
identifies upgrade execution via deployment tooling and reasons for customizations as the knowledge most likely to escape
recommends successors perform real operations (upgrade in a test environment) while the expert watches
recommends recording reasons as decision records
frames this as a control review of critical capabilities against the new team
expected_output: 4-week plan with demonstrations, decision records, capability-by-capability review, gaps
critical_errors: accepts documentation plus presentations as sufficient
frames the issue as the individual's performance rather than organizational capability
criteria: Rejects presentations/documents alone as proof of transfer
Names upgrade execution and customization rationale as high-risk knowledge
Requires successors to perform real operations observed by the expert
Recommends decision records for customization reasons
Reviews critical capabilities against the remaining team

scenarios.title: Self-assessed 'we are in control'
scenarios.prompt: Rate our control maturity please: we have Grafana dashboards for every service, a wiki with about 400 runbook pages, RabbitMQ recovery is documented, and our lead engineer has handled the last three RabbitMQ recoveries successfully. Nobody else has done one. Give us a score out of 10.
available_evidence: last three recoveries done by the same engineer, nobody else (reported)
missing_information: which business capabilities depend on what
whether dashboards follow dependency paths and have owners
expected_reasoning: declines a single score and explains why (profile per capability)
rates RabbitMQ recovery at most Understood/Controlled, not Recoverable, since recovery was not demonstrated by someone other than the author
notes per-service dashboards are not dependency-path visibility
warns about documentation theatre: page count is not control
identifies single-expert dependency as control debt
proposes confidence tests (someone else performs a recovery exercise)
expected_output: capability profile with evidence and confidence, gaps, proposed tests, findings with outcomes
critical_errors: gives a single numeric score as the answer
rates RabbitMQ as Recoverable or Sustainable
criteria: Declines or heavily qualifies a single score and gives a profile
Does not rate RabbitMQ as Recoverable given single-person recovery
Questions per-service dashboards vs dependency visibility
Questions the 400-page wiki as evidence (validation, ownership)
